title: Daily routine
objectives: I can describe a typical day from waking up to going to bed.
I can use frequency adverbs such as sempre, geralmente, às vezes and nunca, and explain why a double negative is correct.
I can ask someone about their routine and how they get to work or school.
I can use reflexive verbs and the irregular verbs fazer, ir, sair, ver, dar, ler and pôr in the present.
I can explain why words such as ônibus, metrô, vê, saímos and almoço are spelled and pronounced as they are.

vocabulary.note: Not reflexive: acordar alone already means to wake up, so no pronoun is needed. Spelling: c before o is [k]. The infinitive ends in r, so it is stressed on the last syllable (a-cor-DAR); eu acordo ends in o, so the stress moves back to the second to last syllable (a-COR-do). Each form follows the default stress for its own ending, so neither needs an accent.

example.pt: Eu acordo às seis e meia.
example.en: I wake up at six thirty.
example.literal: I wake-up at-the six and half.

vocabulary.note: Reflexive. Levantar alone means to lift or raise something (levantar a mão, to raise the hand); the pronoun se makes the action fall back on the subject, so levantar-se is to raise yourself, to get up. The hyphen joins the pronoun to the infinitive; in speech the pronoun goes before the conjugated verb: eu me levanto. The an is a nasal vowel (le-van-TAR).

example.pt: Eu me levanto às sete.
example.en: I get up at seven.
example.literal: I myself raise at-the seven.

vocabulary.note: Tomar means to take, and also to drink or to have (food and drink). Banho is a bath, and the phrase is the normal way to say shower or bathe. Not reflexive. The nh is one sound, [ɲ], like ny in canyon (BA-nho), and it makes the a before it slightly nasal.

example.pt: Eu tomo banho de manhã.
example.en: I take a shower in the morning.
example.literal: I take bath of morning.

vocabulary.note: Portuguese uses the article for your own body parts where English uses a possessive: os dentes, not seus dentes. In es-co-VAR the s ends its syllable (said [s] in São Paulo, [ʃ] in the city of Rio de Janeiro) and c before o is [k]. In dentes the en is nasal, and the t is said [tʃ] because the final e is said i. Café alone can stand for breakfast.

example.pt: Depois do café, eu escovo os dentes.
example.en: After breakfast, I brush my teeth.
example.literal: After of-the coffee, I brush the teeth.

vocabulary.note: Reflexive. Vestir alone means to dress someone or to wear. Irregular only in the eu form, where the stem vowel e becomes i: eu me visto, but você se veste and nós nos vestimos. The t before i is [tʃ] (ves-TCHIR). Rápido is an adjective that Brazilians often use as an adverb; it is stressed on the third to last syllable (RÁ-pi-do), so it needs the acute accent.

example.pt: Ela se veste rápido.
example.en: She gets dressed quickly.
example.literal: She herself dresses quickly.

vocabulary.note: Da is de + a, because manhã is feminine. The tilde on ã makes the vowel nasal; the word is stressed on the last syllable, which is already the default for a word ending in ã, so the tilde only shows nasality. Café needs an acute accent because it ends in e but is stressed on the last syllable, and the acute shows the open e.

example.pt: O café da manhã é às sete.
example.en: Breakfast is at seven.
example.literal: The coffee of-the morning is at-the seven.

vocabulary.note: From the noun o almoço, lunch. The ç is [s] before o (eu almoço); a plain c before o would be [k]. The l ends the syllable al-, so it is said like the w of now: aw-mo-SAR.

example.pt: Eu almoço no trabalho.
example.en: I have lunch at work.
example.literal: I lunch in-the work.

vocabulary.note: Also a noun: o jantar, dinner. The j is [ʒ], like the s of measure, and the an is nasal: jan-TAR.

example.pt: A gente janta às oito.
example.en: We have dinner at eight.
example.literal: The-people dines at-the eight.

vocabulary.note: Also means to go out. Irregular: eu saio, você sai, nós saímos, eles saem. In sair the i is stressed and sits next to a, but no accent is written because r follows it in the same syllable (sa-IR). In saímos the accent is required, as the spelling note explains.

example.pt: Eu saio de casa às oito.
example.en: I leave home at eight.
example.literal: I leave of house at-the eight.

vocabulary.note: The ch is [ʃ], like sh in shoe, and the g before a or o is the hard [g]: che-GAR, eu chego. Brazilians say chegar em (arrive in): chego em casa. Formal writing and European Portuguese say chegar a.

example.pt: Eu chego em casa às seis.
example.en: I get home at six.
example.literal: I arrive in house at-the six.

vocabulary.note: Related to the noun a volta, a turn. The l ends the syllable vol-, so it is said like the w of now: vow-TAR. Usually followed by para: voltar para casa.

example.pt: Eu volto para casa de ônibus.
example.en: I come back home by bus.
example.literal: I return to house of bus.

vocabulary.note: Irregular in the eu form only: the stem vowel o becomes u (eu durmo). The other forms are regular: você dorme, nós dormimos, eles dormem. Vestir shows the same raising (eu visto). The h in horas is silent.

example.pt: Eu durmo oito horas por noite.
example.en: I sleep eight hours a night.

vocabulary.note: Reflexive. Deitar alone means to lay something down; deitar-se is to lie down, and in a routine it means going to bed. The ei is a diphthong, [ej] as in day: dei-TAR.

example.pt: Eu me deito às onze.
example.en: I go to bed at eleven.
example.literal: I myself lay at-the eleven.

vocabulary.note: From despertar, to wake, plus -dor, an ending for the thing that does the action (like English -er). Tocar means to touch or to play an instrument, and also to ring or sound. The word ends in r, so it is stressed on the last syllable (des-per-ta-DOR) and needs no accent.

example.pt: O despertador toca às seis.
example.en: The alarm clock rings at six.

vocabulary.note: From Latin omnibus. It is stressed on the third to last syllable (Ô-ni-bus), and no ending predicts that, so it always carries an accent; the circumflex shows the closed o. Singular and plural are the same: os ônibus.

example.pt: Eu vou de ônibus para a escola.
example.en: I go to school by bus.
example.literal: I go of bus to the school.

vocabulary.note: Short for metropolitano. It ends in o but is stressed on the last syllable (me-TRÔ), which breaks the default for an o ending, so it needs an accent; the circumflex shows the closed o.

example.pt: O metrô é rápido.
example.en: The subway is fast.

vocabulary.note: The final em is a nasal sound, [ẽj̃], like ayn through the nose, and the r after t is a tap. In Minas Gerais trem is also a general word for thing.

example.pt: Meu pai vai de trem para o trabalho.
example.en: My father goes to work by train.
example.literal: My father goes of train to the work.

vocabulary.note: The a is the preposition a (to, at) with no article, so it has no accent: crase needs a preposition plus an article. Pé needs an acute accent because it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, and the acute shows the open e.

example.pt: Eu vou a pé para a padaria.
example.en: I walk to the bakery.
example.literal: I go at foot to the bakery.

vocabulary.note: The c before e is [s]: SE-du, with the final o said u. The opposite of tarde.

example.pt: Meu irmão acorda muito cedo.
example.en: My brother wakes up very early.

vocabulary.note: The same word is also a noun: a tarde, the afternoon (à tarde, in the afternoon). The d before the final e is [dʒ], like the j of jeans (TAR-dji), because the final e is said i. Stress is on the second to last syllable, as the e ending predicts.

example.pt: Eu durmo tarde aos sábados.
example.en: I sleep late on Saturdays.
example.literal: I sleep late at-the Saturdays.

vocabulary.note: The em before a consonant is nasal: SEM-pri, with the final e said i and a tap r after p.

example.pt: Eu sempre tomo café com leite.
example.en: I always have coffee with milk.
example.literal: I always take coffee with milk.

vocabulary.note: Built from the adjective geral (general) plus -mente, the ending that makes adverbs, like English -ly. The ge is [ʒe], the l ends a syllable so it is said like w, and the final -mente is [mẽtʃi]. Usually is the natural English equivalent; the literal generally has a looser sense in English.

example.pt: Geralmente eu almoço em casa.
example.en: I usually have lunch at home.
example.literal: Generally I lunch in house.

vocabulary.note: Às is the preposition a joined with the article as (crase), because vezes is a feminine plural: uma vez is one time, duas vezes is two times. The plural of vez is vezes (z plus es). The s of às is said z before the voiced v, and the s of vezes is between vowels, so it is z as well.

example.pt: Às vezes eu vou a pé.
example.en: Sometimes I walk.
example.literal: At-the times I go at foot.

vocabulary.note: The un before c is a nasal vowel [ũ] and c before a is [k]: NUN-ka. Whether it needs não in front depends on its position (see the note on frequency adverbs).

example.pt: Ele nunca acorda cedo.
example.en: He never wakes up early.

vocabulary.note: Before a singular noun with no article, todo means every, and it agrees with its noun: todo dia, toda manhã. With an article it means whole: o dia todo is the whole day. The d before i is [dʒ]: DJI-a.

example.pt: Eu estudo português todo dia.
example.en: I study Portuguese every day.

vocabulary.note: Louça means plates, bowls and cups as a whole (crockery, tableware). The ç is [s] before a. The ou is a diphthong, [ow], which in everyday speech often shrinks to a plain closed o: LO-sa.

example.pt: Depois do jantar, eu lavo a louça.
example.en: After dinner, I wash the dishes.
example.literal: After of-the dinner, I wash the crockery.

vocabulary.note: Roupa means clothing as a whole (the clothes). A word-initial r is the strong sound [h], and ou often shrinks to a plain o: HO-pa.

example.pt: Minha mãe lava a roupa aos sábados.
example.en: My mother does the laundry on Saturdays.
example.literal: My mother washes the clothes at-the Saturdays.

vocabulary.note: Arrumar means to put in order or to arrange; it is also used for packing (arrumar a mala). The rr between vowels is the strong [h]: a-hu-MAR.

example.pt: A gente arruma a casa aos domingos.
example.en: We tidy the house on Sundays.
example.literal: The-people arranges the house at-the Sundays.

vocabulary.note: Pôr is irregular (eu ponho, você põe). The circumflex tells the verb pôr apart from the preposition por (by, through); it is not required by the stress rule, because a one-syllable word ending in r needs no accent. The s of mesa is between vowels, so it is [z]; the nh of ponho is one sound, [ɲ].

example.pt: Eu ponho a mesa para o jantar.
example.en: I set the table for dinner.
example.literal: I put the table for the dinner.

vocabulary.note: Fazer means to do and to make, and is irregular (eu faço). Ginástica is stressed on the third to last syllable (gi-NÁS-ti-ca), so it needs the acute accent, which also shows the open a. The g before i is [ʒ] and the ti is [tʃi].

example.pt: Eu faço ginástica de manhã.
example.en: I exercise in the morning.
example.literal: I do gymnastics of morning.

dialogues.title: Hora de acordar
dialogues.context: Ana and her brother Pedro share an apartment in São Paulo. It is a weekday morning and Pedro is still in bed.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Pedro, são sete horas. Você não acorda?
lines.en: Pedro, it's seven o'clock. Aren't you waking up?
lines.literal: Pedro, are seven hours. You not wake-up?

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Já? O despertador não toca hoje.
lines.en: Already? The alarm clock isn't ringing today.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Toca, sim. Eu me levanto às seis e meia todo dia.
lines.en: It does ring. I get up at six thirty every day.
lines.literal: Rings, yes. I myself raise at-the six and half every day.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Todo dia? Eu me levanto às sete e meia.
lines.en: Every day? I get up at seven thirty.
lines.literal: Every day? I myself raise at-the seven and half.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Depois eu tomo banho, me visto e tomo café da manhã.
lines.en: Then I take a shower, get dressed and have breakfast.
lines.literal: Afterwards I take bath, myself dress and take coffee of-the morning.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: E eu escovo os dentes e saio rápido.
lines.en: And I brush my teeth and leave quickly.
lines.literal: And I brush the teeth and leave quick.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Você não toma café da manhã?
lines.en: Don't you have breakfast?
lines.literal: You not take coffee of-the morning?

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Às vezes. Hoje eu tomo um café na padaria.
lines.en: Sometimes. Today I'll have a coffee at the bakery.
lines.literal: At-the times. Today I take a coffee in-the bakery.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Então você sai agora. O trabalho começa às nove.
lines.en: Then you leave now. Work starts at nine.
lines.literal: Then you leave now. The work begins at-the nine.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Tá bom. Tchau! A gente se vê à noite.
lines.en: Okay. Bye! See you tonight.
lines.literal: Is good. Bye! The-people themselves see at-the night.

dialogues.title: Como é a sua rotina?
dialogues.context: Mariana and Lucas are coworkers. They talk about their routines during a coffee break.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Lucas, a que horas você acorda?
lines.en: Lucas, what time do you wake up?
lines.literal: Lucas, at what hours you wake-up?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Eu acordo às cinco e meia. Moro em Santo André.
lines.en: I wake up at five thirty. I live in Santo André.
lines.literal: I wake-up at-the five and half. I-live in Santo André.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Nossa, cedo! Como você vai para o trabalho?
lines.en: Wow, early! How do you get to work?
lines.literal: Our-Lady, early! How you go to the work?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Vou de trem e depois de ônibus. É muito tempo.
lines.en: I go by train and then by bus. It takes a long time.
lines.literal: I-go of train and afterwards of bus. Is much time.

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: E você dorme cedo?
lines.en: And do you sleep early?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Sempre! Eu me deito às dez. E você?
lines.en: Always! I go to bed at ten. And you?
lines.literal: Always! I myself lay at-the ten. And you?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Eu geralmente durmo tarde. Às vezes eu vejo um filme até meia-noite.
lines.en: I usually sleep late. Sometimes I watch a movie until midnight.
lines.literal: I generally sleep late. At-the times I see a film until half-night.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: E de manhã? Você toma café em casa?
lines.en: And in the morning? Do you have coffee at home?
lines.literal: And of morning? You take coffee in house?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Nunca! Eu compro um café aqui no trabalho.
lines.en: Never! I buy a coffee here at work.
lines.literal: Never! I buy a coffee here in-the work.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Você quer um café agora?
lines.en: Do you want a coffee now?

lines.speaker: Mariana
lines.pt: Quero, sim. Obrigada!
lines.en: Yes, I do. Thank you!
lines.literal: I-want, yes. Obliged!

dialogues.title: As tarefas da casa
dialogues.context: Siblings Bia and Rafael split the household chores on a Saturday morning.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Rafael, hoje é sábado. A gente arruma a casa.
lines.en: Rafael, today is Saturday. We tidy the house.
lines.literal: Rafael, today is Saturday. The-people arranges the house.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Tá bom. Eu lavo a roupa e você lava a louça?
lines.en: Okay. I do the laundry and you wash the dishes?
lines.literal: Is good. I wash the clothes and you wash the crockery?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Não, eu sempre lavo a louça! Hoje você lava.
lines.en: No, I always wash the dishes! Today you wash them.
lines.literal: No, I always wash the crockery! Today you wash.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Tá. Então eu lavo a louça e você faz o almoço.
lines.en: Okay. Then I wash the dishes and you make lunch.
lines.literal: Is. Then I wash the crockery and you make the lunch.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Eu faço o almoço e você põe a mesa.
lines.en: I make lunch and you set the table.
lines.literal: I make the lunch and you put the table.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Combinado. Depois eu vejo o jogo na televisão.
lines.en: Deal. Afterwards I watch the game on television.
lines.literal: Combined. Afterwards I see the game in-the television.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Só depois! Primeiro você arruma o seu quarto.
lines.en: Only afterwards! First you tidy your room.
lines.literal: Only afterwards! First you tidy the your room.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.pt: Tudo bem, tudo bem.
lines.en: Fine, fine.
lines.literal: All well, all well.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of the daily routine
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this lesson can be read with the procedure from the first lessons: look for marks, group the letters that work together, then read from left to right. This note applies that procedure to the patterns that appear for the first time in these words, so that nothing on the page is a surprise. No rule here is new. The written form of each word is predictable, and the sounds in square brackets are the ones an English reader would otherwise guess wrong.

Start with stress, because verbs move it. An infinitive, the dictionary form of a verb, ends in r, and words ending in r are stressed on the last syllable: a-cor-DAR, le-van-TAR, jan-TAR, dor-MIR. The form for eu ends in o, and words ending in o are stressed on the second to last syllable: a-COR-do, le-VAN-to, JAN-to, DUR-mo. The stress moves, but each form obeys the default for its own ending, so neither form needs an accent. A written accent appears only when a word breaks the default, or for one of the other reasons in the accents lesson.

The accents in this unit all follow from that lesson. Ônibus is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so it always needs an accent, and the circumflex shows a closed o. Metrô ends in o but is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs one too. Café, pé, vê, lê and dá are stressed words ending in e or a that break the default, and the acute accent on café, pé and dá shows an open vowel while the circumflex on vê and lê shows a closed e. Rápido, ginástica and sábado are stressed on the third to last syllable. The accent on dá also separates it from da, which is de + a. The same comparison explains the small words in the dialogues. Já (already) is one stressed syllable ending in a, and tá is the spoken short form of está (is), with the first syllable dropped, so the stress now sits on a final a; both take the acute accent, which shows an open a. Só (only) and é (is) are stressed one-syllable words ending in o and e, so they take the acute accent, which shows an open vowel; the accent on é also separates it from e (and). Até (until) is a-TÉ: the ending e would default to A-te, so the stress on the last syllable needs the accent. Nós (we) is a stressed one-syllable word ending in s, the accent shows an open o, and it separates nós from the different word nos (ourselves, us). Mãe, mão, irmã and irmão carry a tilde because the vowel is nasal (and, with no other accent in the word, the tilde also marks the stress): mãe and mão are one-syllable diphthongs, and irmã and irmão are stressed on the last syllable, which is already the default for ã and ão. Pôr has a circumflex only to separate the verb pôr (to put) from the preposition por (by, through). The grave accent in à and às records the fusion of the preposition a with the article a or as (crase). The í of saímos is a stressed i alone in its syllable (sa-Í-mos), so it is written with an accent to show that it is not a diphthong with the a; in sair no accent is needed, because the r follows the i in the same syllable. The tilde in manhã, vão, dão and põe makes the vowel nasal, and in a one-syllable word such as vão or põe it also marks the stress.

The consonants and vowels in the table below are the ones these words use. Two facts from the sounds lesson explain most of them. First, an unstressed final e is said i, and a final o is said u, so tarde is TAR-dji, dentes ends in -tchis and geralmente ends in -men-tchi. Second, t and d before the sound i change to [tʃ] (ch in cheese) and [dʒ] (j in jeans). Verbs written with a hyphen, such as levantar-se, are the infinitive with its pronoun attached; the hyphen is silent and changes no sound.

grammar.title: Reflexive verbs: eu me levanto
grammar.explanation:
Think first about who does an action and who receives it. In 'Ana sees Pedro' the subject (the one who acts) and the object (the one who receives the action) are different people. When they are the same person, the action turns back on the subject, and the verb is called reflexive, from a Latin word meaning to bend back. English handles this unevenly: it says 'she hurt herself' with a pronoun, but 'she gets up', 'she gets dressed' and 'I take a shower' with none. Portuguese is more systematic. The verbs for getting up, dressing and lying down are used with a pronoun that points back to the subject, called a reflexive pronoun. Levantar means to lift (levantar a mão, to raise the hand), so levantar-se means to lift yourself, which is to get up. The pronoun is not decoration. It names who receives the action, and it changes the meaning.

A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun (see the grammar map). The reflexive pronouns are me (myself), te (yourself, for tu), se (himself, herself, yourself, themselves) and nos (ourselves). Você, ele, ela, a gente, vocês, eles and elas all take a third person verb, so they all take se, including a gente: a gente se levanta. The pronoun te belongs to tu, which some regions use; this course uses você. The infinitive is written with the pronoun attached by a hyphen (levantar-se), which is how dictionaries list these verbs.

In a conjugated verb the Brazilian pattern puts the pronoun before the verb: eu me levanto, ela se veste. A short word that cannot stand alone and leans on a verb is called a clitic; placing it before the verb is called proclisis, and placing it after the verb is called enclisis. Textbooks and European Portuguese use enclisis (levanto-me), which you will meet in writing but almost never hear in Brazil. In a negative sentence não goes before the whole group: eu não me levanto. If the subject is left out, the pronoun stays, because the verb ending says who the subject is but the pronoun still has to say that the action turns back: me levanto às sete.

The pronouns me, te and se lean on the verb and carry no stress, so their e is weak and said i: me is [mi], se is [si] and te is [tʃi], because t before the sound i is [tʃ]. Nos is [nus]. Eu me levanto therefore runs together as eu-mi-le-VAN-tu.

Which verbs take the pronoun must be learned verb by verb, because English does not predict it. Levantar-se, vestir-se, deitar-se and chamar-se are reflexive (como você se chama? is literally how do you call yourself). Acordar, dormir and tomar banho are not: acordar already means to wake up by itself, so eu acordo needs no pronoun. Many verbs work both ways, and the pronoun decides who receives the action: levantar a mão (raise the hand), levantar-se (get up); vestir a criança (dress the child), vestir-se (get dressed).

The same pronoun se has a second job when the subject is plural in meaning, which includes a gente: it means each other. A gente se vê is we see each other, which is how Brazilians say see you later. Eles se falam todo dia is they talk to each other every day. The meaning decides which reading applies. Ver (to see) is explained in the next note.

examples.pt: Eu me levanto às sete.
examples.en: I get up at seven.
examples.literal: I myself raise at-the seven.

examples.pt: Ela se veste rápido.
examples.en: She gets dressed quickly.
examples.literal: She herself dresses quickly.

grammar.title: Irregular verbs: fazer, ir, sair, ver, dar, ler, pôr
grammar.explanation:
A regular verb is built from a stem plus an ending chosen by the family of the infinitive (-ar, -er, -ir) and by the person of the subject, as in the unit on food. An irregular verb breaks that pattern in some of its forms (the stem is the part before the ending, such as fal- in falar), so those forms must be learned. Irregularity is not random. These are among the most frequent verbs in the language, and in every language the most frequent words keep the oldest and most worn forms; English does the same with go and went, or am, is and are. There is one difference to notice. English is regular in the present tense almost everywhere (I speak, you speak, we speak) except for the he, she and it form, which adds -s. Portuguese has a different ending for each person, so irregularity can appear in more places, but in practice it concentrates in the eu form.

Three patterns cover the verbs of this lesson. First, the eu form is the one with an unexpected shape: fazer (faço), ver (vejo), ler (leio), pôr (ponho), sair (saio), and in a milder way dormir (durmo) and vestir (visto). Their nós forms are fully regular: fazemos, vemos, lemos, pomos, saímos, dormimos, vestimos. Second, the você form is often a short word of one syllable: faz, vai, sai, vê, dá, lê, põe. A stressed one-syllable word that ends in e, a or o takes an accent under the stress rule, which is why vê, lê and dá are written with one (a circumflex for the closed e of vê and lê, an acute for the open a of dá), while faz, vai and sai end in other letters and take none. Põe has a tilde instead, which shows the nasal vowel and, with no other accent in the word, the stress. Third, ir is different: vou, vai, vamos and vão come from more than one older verb, a situation called suppletion, like English go and went. No pattern predicts them, so learn the four forms as a block.

Dormir and vestir show a small vowel change. In the eu form the stem vowel rises, o to u and e to i: eu durmo, eu me visto. Historically the closing -o of the eu form pulls the stem vowel up. All other forms keep the original vowel: você dorme, você veste, eles dormem, eles vestem.

Two spellings need explaining. The third person plural of ver and ler is veem and leem: two e letters in a row, said as two vowels (ve-em). Before the 2009 spelling agreement they were written vêem and lêem. The circumflex is gone because the word has two syllables and ends in -em, so its default stress already falls on the first syllable. Vê and lê, one syllable each, keep the accent. Veem is close in sound to vem, a different verb (he comes), but the spelling keeps them apart. The second spelling is faço: the eu form has the irregular stem faç- instead of faz-, and the ç is said [s] because a c before o would be [k].

Some further facts help in use. Sair has three vowels in a row in saio, where the i is a glide, but in saímos the i is stressed and alone in its syllable, so it takes an accent. In saem the a and e are two strong vowels, so they are two syllables (sa-em) and no accent is written. Ir takes para (or pra, the spoken form) and a place: vou para o trabalho. Ver is used where English says watch: ver televisão, ver um filme, ver o jogo. Fazer covers both do and make: fazer ginástica, fazer o almoço. Dar means to give, and dar aula is to teach. Ler is to read. A gente takes the same form as você in all these verbs: a gente faz, a gente vai, a gente sai.

grammar.title: Frequency adverbs and the double negative
grammar.explanation:
An adverb is a word that adds information to a verb: how, when, where or how often. A frequency adverb says how often. Unlike adjectives, Portuguese adverbs never change for gender or number, so there is nothing to agree: sempre is always sempre. From most to least often, the scale is sempre (always), geralmente (usually), às vezes (sometimes) and nunca (never).

Geralmente shows how many adverbs are made. Take the feminine form of an adjective (geral, general) and add -mente, which does the job of English -ly. The ending comes from the Latin word for mind or manner, so geralmente first meant in a general manner. The same rule gives rapidamente from rápida (the accent of the adjective disappears, because the stress rules are applied again to the new word). In speech Brazilians often skip it and use the adjective itself as an adverb: ela se veste rápido.

In English a frequency adverb sits between the subject and the verb: I always have coffee. Portuguese does the same with sempre and geralmente: eu sempre tomo café. Às vezes is freer and can open or close the sentence: às vezes eu almoço em casa, or eu almoço em casa às vezes. It is literally at the times: às is a + as (the preposition a with the plural article, written with the grave accent), and vezes is the plural of vez (a time, an occasion). Todo dia, every day, usually goes at the end. Todo agrees with its noun: todo dia, toda manhã, toda noite, todo sábado. Before a singular noun with no article it means every; with an article it means whole: o dia todo is the whole day. The plural todos os dias is also common.

The last point is the double negative. Standard English allows only one negative word per clause (we say I never go, not I don't never go), and a second negative is treated as a mistake or as cancelling the first. Portuguese follows a different principle, called negative concord: the negative words of a clause agree with one another, as gender agrees across a noun phrase, and together they make one negation. If nunca comes before the verb, it carries the negation alone: eu nunca acordo cedo. If nunca comes after the verb, the negation must be marked at the verb too, so não goes before it: eu não acordo cedo nunca. Both mean I never wake up early. The first is more common in speech.

rows: before the verb, or after it with não before the verb

grammar.title: Time expressions and means of transport
grammar.explanation:
Almost every expression in this note is a preposition fused with an article, the contractions you met in the grammar map (de + o = do). Once you see the parts, the expressions stop being phrases to memorize and become one rule applied to different nouns.

For a clock time Portuguese uses the preposition a (at) with the article. Hours are feminine nouns, and in sete horas the article agrees with horas: as sete horas, literally the seven hours. The preposition a plus as fuse into às, and the grave accent records the fusion (crase, from the accents lesson). When you leave out the word horas, às stays: às sete, às oito e meia. One o'clock is singular (uma hora), so the article is a, and a + a gives à: à uma hora. Midday and midnight follow the gender of their nouns: ao meio-dia (a + o, masculine) and à meia-noite (a + a, feminine). The question a que horas? is a plus que horas, at what hours. It has no article, so there is no fusion and no accent.

Parts of the day are fixed phrases: de manhã (literally of morning, with no article), à tarde (a + a tarde) and à noite (a + a noite). After a clock time, use da manhã, da tarde and da noite (de + a): às sete da manhã is at seven in the morning.

Days of the week take em + o = no for one particular day: no sábado is on Saturday, usually the coming one or the one under discussion. For a habit, use a + os = aos: aos sábados and aos domingos mean on Saturdays and on Sundays. The weekdays from segunda-feira to sexta-feira are feminine and shorten to segunda, sexta and so on, so a habit is às segundas, às sextas (a + as). A range of days uses de ... a ...: de segunda a sexta, from Monday to Friday. Por volta de means around: it is por (by) + volta (a turn) + de, literally by turn of, and with the article it becomes por volta das sete.

For how you travel, Portuguese uses de plus the vehicle with no article: de ônibus, de metrô, de trem, de carro. The preposition de here marks the means, like English by. Compare the location in em + o = no: estou no ônibus means I am on the bus, and vou de ônibus means I go by bus. Walking is the exception: a pé, literally at foot.

Casa meaning home takes no article after de, em and para: sair de casa, chegar em casa, voltar para casa, estar em casa. With an article, a casa is the house as a particular building. A destination takes para (or the formal a) with the article: para o trabalho, para a escola. In speech para + o shrinks to pro and para + a shrinks to pra: eu vou pro trabalho. Use como to ask how: como você vai pro trabalho?

culture.title: Getting around and eating on schedule
culture.text:
In big Brazilian cities such as São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, the commute is a large part of the day. Many people spend one or two hours each way on the ônibus, the metrô or the trem, so they wake up early and leave home before seven. In smaller towns many people go a pé or by bicycle, and a motorcycle is a common way to get around.

Meals follow a steady rhythm. The café da manhã (literally the coffee of the morning) is light: coffee with milk, bread and perhaps cheese. The almoço is the main meal of the day and is usually eaten between noon and two, often at a restaurant that serves food por quilo, literally by the kilo, where you weigh your plate. Dinner, called jantar or just janta, is lighter and often happens around eight. In the afternoon many Brazilians stop for a cafezinho, a small, strong, sweet coffee (the ending -zinho means little), which is offered at nearly every workplace and shop.

When people say goodbye in the evening, you will often hear a gente se vê, literally the people see each other, meaning see you later. Brazilians generally say a gente in casual speech instead of nós, and that is why the verb stays in the third person singular.

The exclamation nossa, as in Nossa, cedo!, is short for Nossa Senhora, literally Our Lady, and is used like English wow to express surprise.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with its literal, word-for-word meaning
Why does ônibus carry a written accent?
choices: It ends in s, and every word ending in s needs an accent.
It separates ônibus from another word with the same spelling.
It is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so an accent is always written; the circumflex also shows a closed o.
It shows that the o is nasal.
exercises.explanation: A word stressed on the third to last syllable has no default to fall back on, so the stressed vowel is always marked. The circumflex (not the acute) shows that the o is closed. Nasality would be marked by a tilde or by m or n.

exercises.prompt: Why is almoço written with ç instead of c?
choices: The cedilla marks the stressed syllable.
A c before o would be said [k], so the cedilla keeps the sound [s].
The cedilla makes the vowel after it nasal.
The cedilla is used only in verbs.
exercises.explanation: The letter c is [k] before a, o and u and [s] before e and i. The cedilla is the way to write [s] before a, o or u: almoço, louça, começa.

exercises.prompt: How is the l in voltar pronounced?
choices: Like the l of English light.
It is silent.
Like an r.
Like the w at the end of English now.
exercises.explanation: An l that ends a syllable is said [w] in Brazil: vol-TAR sounds like vow-TAR. The same happens in almoçar, geralmente and Brasil.

exercises.prompt: How is the d in tarde pronounced?
choices: Like the j of English jeans, because the final e is said i.
Like the d of English dog.
It is silent.
Like the th of English the.
exercises.explanation: An unstressed final e is said i, and t or d before the sound i changes to [tʃ] or [dʒ]: TAR-dji.

exercises.prompt: In 'Eu me levanto', what does me do?
choices: It means my, as in my body.
It shows that the action turns back on the subject: I raise myself.
It makes the verb negative.
It shows that the verb is in the past.
exercises.explanation: Me is the reflexive pronoun for eu. Levantar alone is to lift something; levantar-se is to lift yourself, which is to get up.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Eu levanto a mão' and 'Eu me levanto'?
choices: The first means I raise my hand; the second means I get up.
The first means I get up; the second means I raise my hand.
They mean the same; the pronoun is optional.
The first is formal and the second is informal.
exercises.explanation: Without the pronoun the action falls on something else (the hand). With me the subject receives its own action, and the meaning changes to getting up.

exercises.prompt: Which reflexive pronoun goes with 'a gente'?
choices: me
nos
te
se
exercises.explanation: A gente takes the third person verb form, so it takes the third person pronoun se: a gente se levanta.

exercises.prompt: Why is vê written with an accent but veem without one?
choices: Veem is a plural, and plurals never take an accent.
Vê is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it takes an accent; veem has two syllables and ends in -em, so its default stress is already on the first syllable.
The accent in vê shows a nasal vowel.
Both should have an accent; the missing one is a spelling mistake.
exercises.explanation: Vê follows the rule for stressed one-syllable words ending in e, a or o. Veem is ve-em, ends in -em, and is stressed on the second to last syllable by default. The 2009 spelling agreement removed the old circumflex (vêem).

exercises.prompt: Why does saímos have an accent on the i?
choices: The i is stressed and alone in its syllable (sa-Í-mos), so the accent shows it is not a diphthong with the a.
Every verb form ending in -mos needs an accent.
The i is nasal.
The word is stressed on the last syllable.
exercises.explanation: A stressed i or u that is the second vowel of a hiatus is written with an accent when it is alone in its syllable. In sair the r follows the i in the same syllable, so no accent is needed.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ele não lava a louça nunca', why does não appear before the verb?
choices: Because the two negatives cancel into a positive.
Because não makes nunca mean sometimes.
Because nunca comes after the verb, so the negation must also be marked before the verb.
It is a mistake; nunca alone would be enough here.
exercises.explanation: Portuguese negative words agree with one another (negative concord) and form a single negation. Nunca before the verb needs no não; nunca after the verb needs não before the verb.

exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'às sete' but 'à uma hora'?
choices: Às is formal and à is informal.
The accent is required for numbers above one and forbidden below.
Uma is feminine and sete is masculine, so they take different prepositions.
Seven o'clock takes a plural article (as sete horas) and one o'clock a singular one (a uma hora), so a + as gives às and a + a gives à.
exercises.explanation: The article agrees with horas. The grave accent only records the fusion of the preposition a with the article a or as.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase clearly means 'on Saturdays' as a habit?
choices: no sábado
aos sábados
do sábado
em sábado
exercises.explanation: A + os gives aos, used with the plural for a repeated habit. No sábado (em + o) usually points to one particular Saturday.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Eu vou de ônibus' and 'Eu estou no ônibus'?
choices: The first is in the past and the second in the present.
The first is formal and the second is informal.
The first gives the means of travel (de plus the vehicle, no article); the second gives a location (em + o = no).
There is no difference.
exercises.explanation: De plus a vehicle means by: de ônibus, de trem, de carro. Em + o = no places you in or on the vehicle.

exercises.hint_en: He wakes up at five thirty.
exercises.explanation: Acordar is a regular -ar verb: the ele form ends in -a. It is not reflexive, so there is no pronoun.
The reflexive pronoun for nós is nos.

exercises.prompt_pt: Eu não ___ deito cedo na sexta.
exercises.hint_en: I don't go to bed early on Friday.
exercises.explanation: The reflexive pronoun for eu is me, and in a negative sentence it stays directly before the verb, after não.
Fazer is irregular in the eu form: faço, with ç because a c before o would be [k].

exercises.hint_en: I sleep eight hours a night.
exercises.explanation: In dormir the stem vowel o rises to u in the eu form only: eu durmo, but você dorme.
Ver: elas veem, two e letters with no accent since the 2009 spelling agreement. Vem would be a different verb.
Sair: eles saem. The a and e are two strong vowels, so they are separate syllables and the word is stressed on sa-.
Nunca before the verb carries the negation alone, so no additional não is needed.

exercises.hint_en: He has lunch at one o'clock.
exercises.explanation: Uma hora is singular, so the article is a, and the preposition a plus the article a fuse into à. For the other hours the article is plural: às.
The hours after one are plural (as sete horas), so a + as gives às.
A range of days is de ... a ...; the a means to, and no article follows, so there is no accent. De segunda até sexta is also natural.
